summary: Add and subtract decimals to hundredths by treating the decimal point as the fixed marker of where the same place-value columns continue rightward. The written algorithm is identical to whole-number column arithmetic — align by place value, compose ten hundredths into a tenth when carrying, decompose a tenth into ten hundredths when borrowing — with one new hazard: columns must be aligned by the DECIMAL POINT (tenths under tenths), not by right-edging the digits, and 'ragged' decimals such as 3.4 + 2.78 must be equalised with a placeholder zero (3.40). Learners should estimate first to place the point, compute correctly in both directions including across a zero, and explain WHY lining up the points (not the digits) is necessary.
misconceptions: Aligns the digits by the right edge instead of by the decimal point (3.4 + 2.78 set up wrongly)
Treats the digits after the point as a separate whole number ('longer decimal is bigger', so mis-orders/mis-sets)
Loses or misplaces the decimal point in the answer
Fails to borrow across the tenths, especially with a zero (5.03 - 2.67)
Thinks appending or dropping a trailing zero changes the value

activities.title: Decimal exchange bench: aligning by the point and trading ten-for-one
steps: Set up 3.4 + 2.78 in place-value columns with the decimal point fixed in a central column; notice that 3.4 has an empty hundredths slot (to the right of the 4, above the 8), and add the placeholder zero so it becomes 3.40 with tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths.

Compute 3.45 + 2.78: the hundredths total 13, so fuse ten hundredth-pieces into a single tenth-piece and carry it one column left — exactly the ones-to-tens carry already known. Record the answer 6.23.
Solve 5.03 − 2.67 by decomposing: exchange one whole into ten tenths and one tenth into ten hundredths so you can take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths; record 2.36.
Before each calculation, estimate roughly (3.45 + 2.78 is about 6) and use the estimate to check the point is in the right place afterward.
Re-scale base-ten blocks so a flat = 1, a rod = 0.1, and a small cube = 0.01, and physically trade ten small cubes for one rod to mirror ten-ones-make-a-ten.
activities.insight: Decimals are not a new arithmetic: the point just marks where the columns keep going, and the ten-for-one exchange across every boundary (hundredths→tenths, tenths→ones) is unchanged from whole numbers. You must line up tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths because you can only add like to like.

activities.title: Confronting 'longer-is-larger' with ragged decimals
steps: Decide which is larger, 4.11 or 4.9. Many children wrongly pick 4.11 because it 'looks longer' — but 4.9 is larger. Rewrite with equal places (4.11 vs 4.90) and read them as eleven hundredths versus ninety hundredths to see why.

Decide which is larger, 0.4 or 0.45, and whether 0.4 and 0.40 are equal or different. Then rewrite 0.4 as 0.40 (forty hundredths) to compare the same number of places directly (forty hundredths versus forty-five hundredths).
Build or mark both numbers with hundredths blocks or on a number line, lining up equal place values, and state which is larger and why.
Check the claim 'is 6.18 the same as 6.180?' and justify the answer from place value (appending a trailing zero adds zero in the next place, so the value is unchanged).

Explain in your own words why 2.78 is smaller than 3.4 even though it has more digits and a larger part after the point (0.78 vs 0.40): compare the ones first (2 < 3). Explain why you cannot judge decimal size by counting digits.
activities.insight: The digits after the point are not a separate whole number, so a 'longer' decimal is not automatically larger — 4.9 (nine tenths) is larger than 4.11 (eleven hundredths) despite having fewer digits, while 0.45 (forty-five hundredths) is larger than 0.4 (forty hundredths). You must compare the same place values. Trailing zeros do not change value because they add nothing to any place.

activities.title: Explain why the points must line up
steps: Answer the question 'why must the decimal points line up — what goes wrong if they don't?' in your own words, referring to place value.
Work 5.03 − 2.67 and explain what you did to be able to take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths (decomposing across the tenths and the zero).
Estimate 3.45 + 2.78, 3.4 + 2.78, and 5.03 − 2.67 (about 6, 6, and 2) and describe how each estimate tells you where the point belongs in the exact answer.
Transfer the reasoning to a fresh ragged or zero case you have not seen, setting it up, computing it, and justifying the alignment.
activities.insight: You can only add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths, so aligning by the point keeps like place values together; estimating first lets you catch a misplaced point. Full mastery means justifying the algorithm from place value, not just following steps.

checkQuestion: Give the child these to set out and solve on paper, watching how they align them: 3.45 + 2.78; 3.4 + 2.78; and 5.03 - 2.67. Ask them to estimate each answer first, and for 5.03 - 2.67 to explain why the algorithm works.
checkAnswer: 3.45 + 2.78 = 6.23 (composes ten hundredths into a tenth, ten tenths into a one). 3.4 + 2.78 = 6.18, aligning by the point with a placeholder zero (3.40). 5.03 - 2.67 = 2.36, decomposing across the tenths (and the zero). Estimates about 6, 6, and 2. Explains that the points align because you can only add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.
